cards.explanation: The answer is silent. Asaph says it three ways: "…be not silent; be not speechless; be not still, O God." I bet he's worried, friends, because when you're worried, one way to say it just isn't enough. I think he's asking God to speak up and act.

The answer is cunning. Asaph says "With cunning they scheme against Your people and conspire against those You cherish…" Notice the words "…those You cherish…" Asaph calls them that, and it tells everyone whose people these are.

The answer is that they want to erase Israel as a nation, and it's a heavy one. Asaph quotes them: "Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more." It's not about a little trouble, friends, it's about making Israel disappear. That's why Asaph is praying so hard.

The answer is False. Asaph says "…with one mind they plot together; they form an alliance against You…" They're not arguing over the plan, they're all in on it. A group that agrees that much is a problem.

The answer is God Himself, and look at the wording. Asaph says "they form an alliance against You…" and he's talking to God. So the alliance is against God Himself, friends. Asaph didn't see this as only a fight over land and borders.

The answer is to defeat them like He defeated those enemies. Asaph prays "Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon…" He's pointing at times God already came through and asking for the same again. Smart move, bringing the history into his prayer.

The answer is the pastures of God. The psalm has some people saying, "Let us possess for ourselves the pastures of God." They wanted something that belonged to God. They'd have done better to ask for a cookie, friends.

The answer is True. Asaph prays, "Make them like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind." Chaff is the light stuff that blows away and doesn't stay put. He's asking for the plotters to be scattered.

The answer is His tempest. Asaph says "…so pursue them with Your tempest, and terrify them with Your storm." After the fire on the mountains, he asks for wind and storm to chase them. Two pictures, same prayer, friends.

The answer is seek, and that's the surprise. Asaph asks God to cover their faces with shame "…that they may seek Your name, O LORD." The prayer isn't only about them being stopped, friends. It also asks that they would look for the LORD.

The answer is False. Asaph follows with "May they be ever ashamed and terrified; may they perish in disgrace." He doesn't stop asking after he mentions seeking God's name. Both requests are in his prayer, and I think that's a lot to hold at once.

The answer is that the LORD alone is Most High over all the earth, and what a finish. Asaph prays, "May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth." The whole psalm ends on who God is, friends. Everything else in the prayer leads up to that.
